title: Make them talk
goal: Ledger must not hold a wallet that account has never heard of. That single requirement is what forces the first network call between your services.
startWith: Step 04 finished: two services build from the root, each with its own database.

newIdeas.plain: You declare an interface describing the remote API — method, path, body — and Spring generates the client. No hand-written URL strings, no RestTemplate boilerplate, and the interface doubles as documentation of what you depend on.
The modern synchronous HTTP client in Spring Framework 6.1+. It replaces RestTemplate and backs the generated @HttpExchange client.

Ledger now cannot answer a request unless account answers first. Account's latency is added to yours and account's downtime becomes yours. This is fine, common, and about to hurt — step 06 measures exactly how much.

tasks.do: Declare the account API as an interface in ledger
tasks.why: Writing down what you depend on, as a type, makes the dependency visible and testable.
tasks.how: One interface, one annotation per method. Everything that follows — timeouts, retries, fallbacks — attaches to this one place rather than being spread over the calling code.

blocks.label: ledger: adapter/out/account/AccountClient.java
ledger: config/AccountClientConfig.java

tasks.do: Add POST /api/v1/holds, which validates the wallet with account before writing
tasks.why: This is the first time one service's decision depends on another service's answer.
tasks.how: The use case does three things in order: ask account whether the wallet exists, refuse if not, otherwise write the hold. Keep that logic in the application layer, not in the controller — step 15 will put authorization checks on it and step 10 will wrap it in a transaction.

blocks.label: ledger: domain/model/FundsHold.java
ledger: application/PlaceHold.java — the use case
ledger: adapter/in/web/HoldController.java

check.expect: 201 and a hold with status HELD.

tasks.do: Run both services and watch one request cross the boundary
tasks.why: Seeing a single user action produce log lines in two processes is the moment microservices stop being an abstraction.
tasks.how: Two terminals, two services, two log streams. Account is on 8080, ledger on 8081. Keep both visible — you will be watching them again in step 06 for a less happy reason.

blocks.label: Terminal 3 — a wallet that does not exist, which must be refused
Prove nothing was written for the bad wallet
blocks.body:
docker exec -it lf-postgres psql -U ledgerflow -d ledger \
  -c 'SELECT wallet_code, status FROM funds_holds ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;'

tasks.do: Write an integration test for the cross-service path
tasks.why: You want this covered without needing account to actually be running.
tasks.how: Stub the client interface. This is the payoff for declaring the dependency as a type: the test replaces one bean and never opens a socket. Testing the real HTTP contract between the two is what step 17's contract testing is for.

blocks.label: ledger: src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/PlaceHoldIT.java

proof.expect: A 4xx problem+json, and no row in funds_holds.
proof.note: Two processes, one user action. Ledger is now unable to answer without account — write that sentence down, because step 06 is about what it costs.

doneWhen: Ledger refuses to hold a wallet that account does not know about, and the integration test covers it without account running.

lessons.title: Split the editor
lessons.teach: Right-click a tab → Split Right. Caller on the left, callee on the right — the fastest way to keep a client and its server side by side while you make them agree.
